items.title: Focus Groups With American Indian/Alaska Native Adults to Discuss Substance Misuse and Access to Services.
items.authors: Woods C, Bingham-Hendricks C, Peters-Mosquera A, Miller J, Aronowitz T.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: After the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, there was a 53% increase in overdose deaths in the U.S., with the highest rates among American Indian/Alaska Natives (AI/AN) individuals compared with all racial/ethnic groups in the U.S. Historical trauma has been linked to substance use among AI/AN individuals. First cited in the 1990s, historical trauma is an intergenerational response to the loss of AI/AN communities' land, peoples, and culture secondary to colonization in North America. Two-Eyed Seeing is the gift of multiple perspectives treasured by many Indigenous peoples, which includes storytelling. The purpose of this study was to hear from the tribal members their concerns related to substance use among youth and their ideas related to prevention and treatment.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: The study design was a focus group methodology. Five focus groups were completed with 20 AI/AN self-identified adults over 18 years of age.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Several themes emerged that focused on both prevention and treatment of substance use disorder. Participants expressed concern about their invisibility in state and federal datasets, lack of access to health care, and a lack of prosocial opportunities for youth to inspire their future aspirations. They expressed concern about stigma and the potential negative influences of peers and social media. Two approaches many participants felt could help were to start prevention projects early with elementary-aged youth and to take an intergenerational approach.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: To more broadly understand the needs of the AI/AN medication for opioid use disorder clients, future investigations should include interviews with substance use disorder clients and their families. Further understanding of the experiences of individuals with substance use disorder and their treatment could advance creative treatment plans that are trauma-informed and culturally sensitive. Implementing community participatory action increases the assurance that the needs of AI/AN families are addressed.

items.title: Functional Analysis and Quality Assessment of Mobile Applications for Managing Alcohol Use Disorder.
items.authors: Lee Y, Seo JM.

sections.heading: Aims
sections.text: This study investigated the current mobile applications (apps) for the management of alcohol use disorder (AUD) and analyzed their functionality and quality.

sections.heading: Design/methods
sections.text: A comprehensive search of the Apple App Store and Google Play Store was conducted between August 1 and October 31, 2023, based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, to identify apps specifically designed for patients with AUD. Two independent raters evaluated the apps using the Mobile App Rating Scale and the Institute for Healthcare Informatics functionality score.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: This search resulted in the selection of 33 apps for assessment. The Mobile App Rating Scale quality assessment indicated that more than half of the selected apps were suitable for use, and the Institute for Healthcare Informatics functionality assessment determined that the apps had a 4.5 average for 11 possible functions. Additionally, a detailed analysis of the top three apps with the highest scores for both quality and functionality was conducted. This study highlighted the key features that apps for AUD management should incorporate and identified possible areas for improvement.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Based on these results, we recommend that apps record and store data on the number of days to abstinence and the amount of alcohol consumed and display this information using graphs. In addition, we recommend that apps allow users to customize the timing and number of reminders and alarms and connect to a support system or professional immediately in high-risk situations.

items.title: "Daily Growth" Parenting Program Delivered via Ecological Momentary Intervention: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial of a Prototype.
items.authors: Ewald S, Berkowitz TS, Hiskens-Ravest S, Bufton K, Bates M, O E, Fuller-Tyszkiewicz M, King GL, Westrupp EM.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Despite evidence showing that parenting interventions reduce rates of child mental health problems, their reach and engagement remain low. Daily Growth is a digital parenting program designed to improve parent and child emotion regulation using an ecological momentary intervention (EMI) approach. Daily Growth sends twice-daily prompts and delivers 3-minute videos tailored to a recent parenting situation, offering 2 program types (Emotion Coaching and Active Play) to meet different parent preferences. EMI has rarely been tested with parenting programs.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This pilot aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the EMI design and a prototype of Daily Growth, offering the 2 programs via 10 of 60 planned videos.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A pilot randomized controlled trial recruited 189 Australian parents of children aged 2-4 years, randomized to either intervention (n=94) or active control (n=95). Participants completed a 25-minute online survey at baseline and at conclusion of the program period. In the intervening 2 weeks, participants received twice-daily 1-minute pre-EMI surveys via email. Participants who reported any parent or child negative affect or emotion dysregulation received a resource. Participants in the intervention condition were randomized in the moment to receive a 3-minute Emotion Coaching or Active Play video, while participants in the control condition received a link to a parenting website. Participants were sent a 1-minute post-EMI survey. For both conditions, parenting support was tailored to 1 of 5 predefined parenting situations.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Overall, 71% (135/189) of participants completed the 2-week post survey, and over two-thirds completed at least half of the daily pre-EMI surveys. Despite technical issues, most participants would recommend Daily Growth to other parents (53/67, 79%), use the skills learned (46/67, 69%), reported it as easy to use (45/67, 67%), and were satisfied with Daily Growth (40/67, 60%).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This pilot evaluated whether brief EMI resources could engage parents in real time. Findings suggest that the Daily Growth prototype was feasible and well received, supporting further implementation in a larger trial.
